title: Partial Differential Equations
body:
A differential equation in a function of **several** variables, so the derivatives in it are
[[Partial Derivative|partials]]. An ODE describes something changing in time; a PDE describes
something changing in time **and** varying in space, which is most of physics.

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = k\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}
$$

The unknown $u(x,t)$ is a whole field: a temperature at every position and every moment. Where an
ODE's general solution carried $n$ arbitrary constants, a PDE's carries arbitrary **functions**,
which is why boundary conditions rather than initial values do most of the work here.

## The three of this course

| Equation | Name | Models | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| $u_t = k\,u_{xx}$ | [[Heat Equation]] | diffusion, smoothing out | parabolic |
| $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ | [[Wave Equation]] | vibration, propagation | hyperbolic |
| $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$ | [[Laplace's Equation]] | steady state, equilibrium | elliptic |

They are close relatives on paper and behave completely differently: the first smooths any initial
roughness away, the second carries it along forever, and the third has no time in it at all.
Laplace's equation is what the other two settle down to once $\partial/\partial t = 0$.

## Separation of variables

The one solution method in this block. Assume the answer factors:

$$
u(x,t) = X(x)\,T(t)
$$

Substitute, then divide by $XT$ until each side of the equation depends on **one** variable only. A
function of $x$ can equal a function of $t$ for all $x$ and $t$ only if both are the same constant,
so:

$$
\frac{T'}{kT} = \frac{X''}{X} = -\lambda
$$

and the PDE has become **two ODEs**, which is why block 3 comes first. The boundary conditions turn
the $X$ equation into an eigenvalue problem: only certain $\lambda$ admit a nonzero solution, and
those are the modes. Superpose them, and matching the initial condition means expanding it in those
modes, which is a [[Fourier Series]].

**That is the link to [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] and it is not incidental**: separation of
variables produces a basis of [[Orthogonal Functions]], and Fourier coefficients are how you write
your particular initial condition in that basis. Same "expand in a basis" move as
[[Diagonalization]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] and as [[Systems of Differential Equations]], one more
dimension up.
